text.p: Canada's proposal to maintain curbs on foreign ownership of telephone companies may restrict the ability of many of Bell Canada's competitors to raise capital in the markets.

"I think they are really wrong. I think by not changing the foreign ownership rules, it really restricts the ability of this industry to bring capital into Canada," Juri Koor, chief executive of Call-Net Enterprises Inc, told Reuters.

Canada offered on Tuesday to the World Trade Organization talks on telecommunications to end Teleglobe Inc's monopoly on overseas traffic by October 1, 1998, and liberalize the carriage of international traffic by the end of 1999.
But there was no change in Canada's position on foreign ownership on which the United States had pressed hard.
Eamon Hoey, a telecommunications consultant at Hoey Associates, said Canada was right to resist bowing to the U.S. government's pressure.

"My view is that the government of Canada certainly in this particular instance has the right attitude in playing hardball with the Yanks," Hoey said. "The government of Canada has gone a long way in trying to accommodate the United States."

Hoey said the ownership restrictions would make it harder for start-up operations to tap foreign markets on which they often depended because of the reluctance of Canada's conservative investment community to make such investments.

Canada's two largest competitive long-distance carriers, AT&T Canada Long Distance Services and Sprint Canada Ltd, were unlikely to be affected dramatically by the failure to lift the restrictions, executives said.
Koor said the decision was unlikely to change how Sprint Corp felt about its investment in Call-Net.
"I don't think so. They're quite happy with what we are doing," he said.

James Meenan, chief executive of AT&T Canada Enterprises, a unit of AT&T Corp which in turn owns 33.3 percent of AT&T Canada Long Distance, said the decision was unimportant to AT&T's long-distance plans in Canada.
"We have said from day one in our filings that we don't need foreign ownership changes in order to implement our strategy," Meenan said in a telephone interview.

Hoey said the only impact on AT&T Canada Long Distance would be making it harder for the three Canadian banks -- Royal Bank of Canada, Toronto-Dominion Bank and Bank of Nova Scotia -- which own the remaining two-thirds of the holding company -- to sell their equity stakes if they desired.
Canada's mainline phone companies, represented by Stentor, voiced disappointment that the government was waiting as long as October 1998 to end Teleglobe's monopoly.

"The longer the Teleglobe monopoly exists, the longer the customers get denied the benefits of competition," said Carol Stephenson, president of Stentor Resource Centre Inc, which manages Stentor's relations with Teleglobe.
